title: The Summer That Never Happened Again
author: Stinehart, Kevin
summary: Opening with a reader's story about a Wyoming baseball team that kept gathering informally at the ballpark after their season ended—and never did it again—Kevin Stinehart defines the 'childhood commons' as any shared, recurring place where children can meet, move, invent, negotiate, and gradually take ownership of their social world without adult-designed programming. He contrasts organized sports, where adults carry the entire structure, with child-led free play on the same field after the season ends: the bases haven't moved, but the developmental environment has, because now the children must decide who plays, what counts as fair, and what to do when someone is bossy or left out. The essay argues that the commons disappeared not because families stopped valuing it but because it was a collective resource no single family can recreate alone. Adults are not absolved: they need to 'hold the edges'—providing safety, food, and access—without occupying the center, because the developmental damage comes when adult instincts for improvement transform a loose gathering into another adult-designed program. The essay closes with practical, small-scale examples of how communities can rebuild the commons and urges readers to put recurring unstructured time on the calendar before the moment passes.
points: The 'childhood commons' is not just unstructured play—it is unstructured play that recurs in the same place with the same community, allowing belonging to grow through return rather than through single engineered experiences.

Organized sports and child-led free play do fundamentally different developmental work: organized sports teach execution within a designed structure, while free play develops the judgment required to sustain a social world that belongs to the children.

The decline of the childhood commons is not a family-by-family choice but a collective action problem: opening the front door gains nothing when every other child is at tutoring, practice, or inside on a screen.

Adults need to 'hold the edges'—supply safety, food, and access—without occupying the center; the developmental damage comes when adult instincts for improvement transform a loose gathering into another adult-designed program.
Communities can rebuild the commons through small, predictable invitations: same place, same time, every week, open to whoever shows up—the children will take it from there.
quotes: But 'it never happened again' revealed something much larger. That summer had become a small fossil from a nearly vanished world: a piece of the childhood commons.
Children did not need an playdate to enter those worlds. They only needed to show up and find someone else there.
During the season, the goal was to play baseball correctly. Afterward, the goal was to keep the afternoon alive.

That distinction matters. Keeping a game alive requires judgment. Children must bend without surrendering everything, lead without driving everyone away, include less-skilled players without destroying the game, survive bad calls, and decide which disagreements matter enough to stop for.

We often talk about the decline of free play as though families simply stopped valuing it. That explanation is convenient, but it misses the collective nature of the problem. One family cannot create a neighborhood full of children.
A single afternoon creates a memory. A repeated afternoon creates a culture.
Adult withdrawal is not the goal. The goal is adult presence that leaves enough room for children to become consequential.
Children need places where the stakes are low enough to recover from mistakes but real enough that their choices matter.

We’re good at recognizing childhood in retrospect. We call it magical, take pictures, and talk about how wonderful it was to see the kids off their devices. We are less practiced at protecting its return.
